posts.body_html:
BaseDrifter: I always heard that rumor, but not sure if this is what happens in Sarracenia. So far, it seems the genetics of both parents rather than gender determines the frequency of what genes are dominant in the offspring. However, I wouldn't be surprised if some crosses with one mother but mutiple fathers did show the mother's features as dominant in most or all crosses. Some genes are really "stronger" and tend to get passed on more frequently. However, I think the same thing can be said for the father donor as well: if the father genes are really "strong" it shows up very easily.

Check out my little rascal:my relatives said they could spot the "Wang" gene from miles away:



The overall shape and "cheekyness" comes from the wang genes. Her half moon eyes, though, we're still trying to figure that one out:

posts.body_html:
calen: yeah, we call her mini-me sometimes, or Improved Mike Wang...she's a good looking version of me, haha!

Thanks Eric! You know well, they grow up so quickly...seems like just a few months ago she could be held with one hand (the "football hold"), and now she barely fits in the car seat.

Thanks Pokie! Sorry, what wasn't pictured is that famous red label in her crib saying "not for sale."

Basedrifter: Actually, I'm pretty sure you can make multiple different crosses using one flower, although it's not a common practice because it's hard to both label and figure out which lobe of the seed pod is from which cross. Also, crack the seed pod the wrong way during harvest time and it'll all get mixed up.
